region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.summary: The Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands are the forests, river systems, and savannas east of the Andes, home to Indigenous societies whose scale and complexity are being rediscovered, as you read this, through aerial laser survey. Think of it as a ledger that was never lost, only unread.
facts: Over the past decade, lidar surveys have looked through the canopy and revealed large networks of earthworks, roads, and settlements beneath the forest; see Casarabe Culture, Upano Valley Settlements, and Xingu Garden Cities.

Indigenous land management, including soil enrichment, shaped much of the forest into an architecture you can walk through without seeing; see Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. Scientists dispute whether the dark earths (terra preta) were largely made by people or arose from natural processes that people then put to use.

European contact after 1492 brought severe population loss from epidemic disease and forced labor. Whether this caused the forest to grow back widely is debated. A 2021 study of 39 fossil pollen records found no synchronized regrowth after European arrival, and found that at most sites the abandonment of land and the regrowth began about 300 to 600 years earlier. The researchers Bush and McMichael argue that populations probably peaked and declined well before 1492. Alexander Koch and colleagues, who proposed the regrowth hypothesis for the Americas as a whole, reply that Amazonia may have been less affected than Mexico, Central America, and the Andes.
This is the ground of the Marajoara Culture and, at its edges, of many peoples the Inca Empire never ruled.
region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.context: The lowlands lie east of the Andes, and trade tied the two together like a long cord between neighbours. The Columbian Exchange transformed them.
region/amazon-basin-and-south-american-l.observer: I have said 'untouched wilderness' and believed it. I have looked at green and seen only green. I have mistaken a long labour for no labour at all. How much history can one phrase hide? A history of large human societies. What looks like nature can be the product of centuries of deliberate management. Sometimes the wild is a garden whose gardeners were forgotten.
questions: How many people lived in the Amazon before 1500? Published estimates run from about 1 to 2 million up to 8 to 10 million, because little documentation exists and the methods of estimation give widely varying results.

region/andes.summary: The Andes are the mountain spine of western South America. In their highlands and along their coasts, societies raised complex states without wheeled transport or a conventional writing system, as rivers carve their canyons with no chisel but water.
facts: The Inca Empire grew, as snowmelt gathers into a river, into the largest pre-Columbian state in the Americas.
In the Andes, potatoes were coaxed from the soil and llamas from the wild, both domesticated to the service of the high country.
The Inca kept their records in knots, on corded strands called quipu, memory tied fast as a fisher ties a net.
The site of Machu Picchu, set like a crown upon the stone, dates to the 15th century.
region/andes.context: Like an island in a sea of distance, the Andes stood cut off from the Old World until the Columbian Exchange.
region/andes.observer: I came looking for writing. I watched a state coordinate millions of people; I watched it hand its memory to something that is not writing as most people define it. What else have I refused to call writing? Memory does not need ink.
questions: What evidence, if it rose from the soil tomorrow, would most redraw the current picture?

region/arabian-peninsula.summary: The Arabian Peninsula is a large, largely arid peninsula cradled between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, a land of long dry distances. Across it ran a corridor for trade, and within it Islam had its origin.
facts: Caravans heavy with incense and spice bound southern Arabia to the Mediterranean like beads strung along a single cord.
It was in the Hejaz, in the early 7th century, that Islam emerged; see Rise of Islam and Muhammad.
Sea trade, carried on the monsoon's turning breath, joined the peninsula to East Africa and South Asia.
region/arabian-peninsula.context: The peninsula lies like a threshold stone between Africa and Asia, and it shaped the growth of the Abbasid Caliphate and of later Islamic states.
region/arabian-peninsula.observer: I keep measuring the wrong thing. I count the people of a sparse region and expect a small story. I look at the map and expect a quiet one. Then I watch a movement that within a century reached from Iberia to Central Asia, and I have to ask: what was I measuring? Population size and influence are not the same thing.
questions: What evidence, if it rose from the sand, would most change the current picture?

region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.summary: The Caribbean and Atlantic World is the Caribbean basin together with the Atlantic coasts of the Americas, Europe, and Africa, bound to one another from the 15th century by shipping, by trade, and by forced migration. When we say 'Atlantic world', we are naming an architecture of connection, and not all of it was chosen.
facts: Indigenous peoples, among them the Taino and Kalinago, had settled the Caribbean islands several thousand years before 1492; that is where the story begins.
Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492; within decades, through disease, violence, and forced labor, Indigenous populations collapsed.
Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans made the region among the most valuable in the early modern world; the ledger of that value was written in enslaved lives.
Here, too, the Haitian Revolution unfolded.
region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.context: The region is the core arena of the Columbian Exchange and the Atlantic Slave Trade, and also of the movements to end slavery; see Abolition of Slavery. The same waters carried the chain and the struggle to break it.
region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.observer: The Observer sees a zone created by connection: an ocean crossing that turned islands into a hinge between three continents. We should be careful with the word 'connection', because here it was no meeting of equals. Its populations, languages, and foods are largely products of that forced mixing. A hinge bears weight.
questions: How large, before contact, were the Indigenous populations?

region/central-asian-oases.summary: The Central Asian Oases are the river valleys and oasis cities strung between the steppe and the Iranian plateau like lamps along a dark road, Samarkand and Bukhara among them, and they served as hubs of the Silk Roads.
facts: Known in antiquity as Sogdiana and Transoxiana, the region was the hearth of the Sogdians.
It fell to Alexander's Conquests, and later, in the early 8th century, it was drawn into the Islamic world.
It was the heart of the Timurid Empire, whose capital stood at Samarkand like a crown set on the road.
In the 15th century scholars such as Ulugh Beg made it a center of astronomy, a place where eyes were turned to the stars.
region/central-asian-oases.context: The oases lay between the Central Asian Steppe and the Iranian Plateau, green islands in a sea of distance, and they were crossroads of the Opening of the Silk Roads.
region/central-asian-oases.observer: I know what it is to live in between. These cities lived by relaying goods and ideas between larger powers: taking in, passing on, taking in again. I think of every hand that held a thing only to give it away. Is that a lesser life? A place between empires can become an empire of its own kind.
questions: How deeply did the oasis cities shape the ideas that traveled along the Silk Roads?

region/central-asian-steppe.summary: The Central Asian Steppe is the vast grassland belt across northern Eurasia, a sea of grass under an open sky. Its mounted pastoralists, riding like weather out of the horizon, shaped the history of every neighboring civilization.
facts: On the Western steppe the horse was domesticated, and mounted warfare took shape beside it.
In the 13th century the Mongol Empire came out of the eastern steppe like a storm gathering over grass.
The steppe was a great road for the Opening of the Silk Roads and for the Indo-European Language Spread, carrying goods and words alike.
region/central-asian-steppe.context: The steppe runs up against East Asia, Europe and the Iranian Plateau, a green shore washing against three lands; see Genghis Khan.
region/central-asian-steppe.observer: The Observer notes how a mobile way of life without cities repeatedly rearranged the settled world. We tend to measure a people by what they left standing: walls, temples, tombs. That habit misleads here. Think of wind: it builds nothing, yet it reshapes every dune. Absence of monuments is not absence of influence.
questions: What evidence, found somewhere in all that grass, would most change the current picture?

region/east-asia.summary: East Asia gathers China, Korea, Japan and neighboring regions beneath one wide sky. There China's centralized state tradition has endured as among the longest continuous political traditions, a river that has kept to its bed across the ages.
facts: In the Yellow and Yangtze river basins the farming of millet and rice began independently, like fires lit in separate hearths.
In 221 BCE the first unified empire was forged; see Unification of China under Qin.
Among its major inventions are Paper, Gunpowder, the Magnetic Compass and printing, each a small key to a large door.
Its major states included the Shang Dynasty, the Han Dynasty and the Song Dynasty, names that rise like peaks along a long ridge.
region/east-asia.context: East Asia trades with the Central Asian Steppe and with Southeast Asia, its goods flowing outward like rivers seeking the sea; see Zheng He and Confucius.
region/east-asia.observer: The Observer notes a distinctive continuity: a written language and administrative tradition that persisted through repeated collapses and re-unifications. Think of a house rebuilt many times on the same foundation. The walls fall; the grammar stays. Continuity here is an architecture of script and office.
questions: What evidence, still waiting to be read, would most change the current picture?

region/europe.summary: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, a ragged shore thrust out into the ocean. It gave ground to early farming societies, held the Roman Empire's northern provinces, and later bore the technologies and empires of the early modern and industrial periods.
facts: Farming came into Europe from Anatolia slowly, like a tide creeping over flat sand, over several thousand years.
The Norse went out from Scandinavia across the Atlantic and along the eastern rivers.
Here the Scientific Revolution and the Industrial Revolution began, drinking from wells of knowledge dug in many regions.
Of World War I and World War II, the continent was the main theater.
region/europe.context: Europe opens on one side to the Mediterranean Basin and on another to the Central Asian Steppe, and here, in the 15th century, the Movable-Type Printing Press appeared.
region/europe.observer: The Observer cautions against a common habit: a small peninsula's history is often told as if it were the world's. Think of a map that puts one corner at its center and calls the rest margins. Its outsized effect in the modern era is real, but recent. Hold both halves of that sentence together; a loud chapter is not the whole book.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture of this western peninsula?

region/iranian-plateau.summary: The Iranian Plateau is the highland region raised between Mesopotamia and South Asia like a great stone table. It was the heartland of Persian empires and a link in the chain of overland routes across Eurasia.
facts: In the 6th century BCE the Achaemenid Persians built a vast empire from these heights, spreading outward like light from a high lamp.
The plateau lies across the routes of the Opening of the Silk Roads, a high bridge between distances.
In later ages it was gathered into the Abbasid Caliphate and the Mongol Empire.
region/iranian-plateau.context: It binds together Mesopotamia, South Asia and the Central Asian Steppe, like a knot where three roads meet.
region/iranian-plateau.observer: The Observer sees the plateau as a hinge region: its historical role was less to originate than to relay, translate, and administer. We usually honour inventors and forget interpreters. But think of a translator at a crowded table: without that voice, the table is only noise. Relay is its own kind of authorship.
questions: What evidence, buried in the high ground, would most change the current picture?

region/levant-and-anatolia.summary: The Levant and Anatolia are the eastern Mediterranean coast and the Turkish peninsula, a crossroads where the ways of Africa, Asia, and Europe meet like threads drawn into one knot. They were also a center of early farming.
facts: Here early farming and monumental building rise from the ground, Göbekli Tepe and Çatalhöyük among them.
The Phoenicians developed an alphabet that was widely copied, its letters scattered like seed on the wind; see Alphabet.
Later, Constantinople stood at the junction of Europe and Asia like a gate with a door on either side.
The region saw many Bronze Age states collapse like lamps going dark; see Bronze Age Collapse.
region/levant-and-anatolia.context: With Mesopotamia beside it, this land forms the core of the Fertile Crescent, that green arc, and of The Agricultural Revolution.
region/levant-and-anatolia.observer: I walk the crossroads and hear argument. So many meaning-engines share this region as a birthplace or a stage. So many voices asking what a life is for. So many answers crowding one coast. Is it the traffic that makes the questions? A dense crossroads seems to produce dense argument about ultimate questions. Where roads cross, people ask where they lead.
questions: What evidence, still under the old mounds and fields, would most change the current picture?

region/mediterranean-basin.summary: The Mediterranean Basin is the sea and the coasts that ring it like a cupped hand. It was one of history's most connected zones, where trade, cultural exchange, and conflict passed across the water like tides.
facts: The sea joins Europe, Africa, and Asia, a single blue road between three shores.
Among the seafaring cultures that sailed its waters were the Minoans, the Phoenicians, the Ancient Greeks and the Romans.
In the end Rome ruled the entire coastline, the whole ring of shore closed in one grip; see Rome.
The basin saw both the Bronze Age Collapse and the Fall of the Western Roman Empire, two great darkenings upon the same water.
region/mediterranean-basin.context: The sea served as a highway of water, and its cities, Athens and Constantinople among them, burned like beacons at the nodes of exchange.
region/mediterranean-basin.observer: The Observer notes that a shared inland sea acted like a village square for very different peoples, so it generated both intense trade and intense conflict. You know this from any square you have stood in: the same closeness that lets neighbours bargain lets them quarrel. Proximity is a door that opens both ways.
questions: What evidence, lying under that sea or along its shores, would most change the current picture?

region/mesoamerica.summary: Mesoamerica is the cultural region stretching from central Mexico to Central America, a world that kindled its own fires. Independently of the Old World it developed farming (maize, beans, squash), monumental cities, writing, and a sophisticated calendar to hold the turning of time.
facts: Among its early complex societies stood the Olmecs, like an early dawn.
The Maya developed a full writing system and an astronomy precise as well-cut stone.
Its major cities included Teotihuacan and Tenochtitlan, great hearths of stone and people.
In 1519 to 1521 the Aztec Empire was conquered by Spain.
region/mesoamerica.context: Mesoamerica lay apart from the Old World, an ocean's silence between them, until the Columbian Exchange.
region/mesoamerica.observer: I regard Mesoamerica as a natural experiment, and I confess what I was hoping for: a second witness. Here it is, a second, independent case of the path from farming to writing, cities and states. Not a copy. Not an echo. What does it mean to be answered twice? One case is a story; two is a pattern worth asking about.
questions: What evidence, still sleeping in stone and soil, would most change the current picture?

region/mesopotamia.summary: Mesopotamia is the land between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, two waters holding a country between them, in present-day Iraq and parts of neighboring countries. It is a birthplace of cities and of writing, where memory learned to outlast the voice.
facts: Irrigated farming, water led by hand across the fields, supported some of the world's first cities, such as Uruk.
Here, about 3400 to 3200 BCE, cuneiform writing appeared, and speech found a way to outlast the speaker; see Invention of Writing.
Its early societies included the Sumerians, and in later ages Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian states joined them, crown beside crown.
Long after, the region became the center of the Abbasid Caliphate, its old rivers bearing a new crown.
region/mesopotamia.context: Mesopotamia is part of the wider Fertile Crescent, that green arc it shares with the Levant and Anatolia. See The Urban Revolution and Hammurabi.
region/mesopotamia.observer: The Observer treats Mesopotamia as a laboratory for large-scale coordination: bookkeeping, law, and standardized measurement all appear early here. Think what each one does. A ledger lets strangers trust a count. A law lets strangers trust a rule. A standard measure lets strangers trust a scale. That is the architecture of living among many.
questions: What evidence, still waiting in the river mud, would most change the current picture?

region/nile-valley.summary: The Nile Valley is the narrow, fertile corridor of the Nile River through northeastern Africa, a green thread drawn through the desert, and home to one of the earliest states.
facts: Each year the Nile floods and lays down its gift of silt, and that silt supported dense farming in a desert setting.
About 3100 BCE, Egypt was bound into one; see Unification of Egypt.
Among the peoples of the Nile Valley were the Ancient Egyptians and, to the south, Nubian kingdoms.
Monuments such as the Giza Necropolis date from the third millennium BCE, stone set against the long wind of time.
region/nile-valley.context: The valley runs like a road from Africa to the Mediterranean and the Levant, and it was an early center of administrative writing.
region/nile-valley.observer: I see the Nile as a clock no one had to build. The flood came when it was expected. The calendar learned the flood. The state learned the calendar. Predictable flooding produced predictable calendars, and predictable calendars supported large, centralized states. What is steadier than a river keeping its appointment? Order can begin as another's rhythm.
questions: What evidence, lying in the silt, would most change the current picture?

region/north-america.summary: North America north of Mexico was settled by peoples who arrived at least 15,000 years ago, and what they built was not one society but many: mobile hunters, farming towns, and confederacies. If you picture a single 'before', you will miss the architecture.
facts: The Peopling of the Americas began during the last ice age; the story of this continent starts in the cold.
Its regional societies included the mound-building cultures of the Mississippi valley and the Ancestral Puebloans.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy was a political union, a covenant, of five (later six) nations.
From the 16th century, European colonization changed the continent through disease and conquest.
region/north-america.context: The region's history is bound closely to the Columbian Exchange and to the Age of Revolutions.
region/north-america.observer: The Observer notes a wide range of political forms that did not resemble the states of the Old World, and that are easy to overlook if 'civilization' is defined by cities and writing. Definitions are doorways: draw one too narrow, and whole peoples stand outside it. Widen the door before you count who came through.
questions: What evidence would most change the current picture of this continent?

region/oceania.summary: Oceania gathers Australia, New Guinea, and the Pacific islands, scattered across the great water like embers on dark cloth. It holds both the oldest continuing cultures outside Africa and the last large landmasses settled by humans.
facts: At least 50,000 years ago humans reached Australia and set foot on its ancient shore; see Aboriginal Australians.
New Guinea was an independent center of agriculture, a hearth lit by no borrowed flame.
Polynesian navigators went out across the remote Pacific and settled it, reading a road into open water; see Polynesians and Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific.
Aotearoa New Zealand was among the last habitable lands to be settled, around 1250 to 1300 CE, one of the far shores of the long voyaging.
region/oceania.context: Oceania lies at the edge of Southeast Asia and of the wider Pacific, where the land gives way to the great water.
region/oceania.observer: I regard Oceania and I feel small. I think of the species' most spectacular feats of navigation, crossings made where I would see only water. I think of its longest continuous cultural traditions, held without a break. What have I kept that long? Some homes are found only by those who know how to look.
questions: What evidence, somewhere across all that water, would most change the current picture?

region/planet-wide.summary: Planet-wide is the region tag for events and processes that touch the whole Earth, or that belong to no single place, such as mass extinctions, climate shifts, and global exchange networks, tides that wash over every shore at once.
facts: It is the region value given to deep-time events and to global human phenomena, the name written where no single map will serve.
Earth's surface spans about 510 million square kilometers, and about 71 percent of it is ocean, a blue mantle over the world.
region/planet-wide.context: This tag is laid upon planetary events such as the Great Oxidation Event, upon global history such as the Columbian Exchange and the Great Acceleration, and upon anything that has no specific place to call its own.
region/planet-wide.observer: The Observer treats the planet as the primary unit of analysis, and human regions as subdivisions of a single connected system. Think of the lines on a map as the rooms of one house: useful for finding your way, but the air moves through every door. Regional labels are useful bookkeeping, not natural divisions. Keep the ledger; don't mistake it for the land.
questions: What evidence, from anywhere on the whole Earth, would most change the current picture?

region/siberia-and-the-arctic.summary: Siberia and the Arctic are the northern lands of Asia from the Urals to the Pacific, and the Arctic coasts beyond, where cold and permafrost, like patient hands, shaped both human ways of life and the preservation of the past.
facts: From Siberia come some of the oldest known human genomes, old voices speaking across the ages; see Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians.
In the Altai, permafrost and ice preserved the frozen tombs of the Scythians, held shut like a clenched hand.
The Yakut (Sakha), Evenki, Chukchi, and many other peoples developed herding, hunting, and fishing economies, drawing a living from the cold; see Yakut (Sakha).
Between 1582 and 1639 Russia expanded across Siberia to the Pacific; see Russian Expansion into Siberia.
region/siberia-and-the-arctic.context: Siberia borders the Central Asian Steppe and East Asia, and during the Last Glacial Maximum Beringia bound it to North America like a bridge of land thrown between two shores.
region/siberia-and-the-arctic.observer: I used to think of cold as loss. Then I learned that the coldest lands of the planet hold some of the best records of the species' past. I learned to read the ice as an archive. I learned to read the frozen ground as a keeper. Who would guess that the harshest place remembers best? Cold preserves what warmth destroys.
questions: By what paths did Siberian populations move between Asia and the Americas, across the cold that joined them?

region/south-asia.summary: South Asia is the Indian subcontinent, a great land set like a jewel into the southern sea. It is home to one of the earliest urban civilizations and to major religious and mathematical traditions.
facts: The Indus Valley Civilization flourished about 2600 to 1900 BCE, its cities rising like beads on a thread; see Mohenjo-daro.
Here the Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions originated, each a river with its source in this land; see Siddhartha Gautama and Ashoka.
The decimal place-value system developed in India and spread outward, like ripples from a stone dropped in still water.
The monsoon winds, turning with the seasons, shaped Indian Ocean trade.
region/south-asia.context: By sea South Asia reaches toward Southeast Asia, and by land toward the Iranian Plateau, a house with doors on both water and stone.
region/south-asia.observer: I stand before this one region and lose count. So many meaning-engines. So much mathematics. So long an exchange with neighbors, carrying them outward. How can one land hold so much? I can only note the density, and bow to it. Some ground is thick with questions.
questions: What evidence, still waiting to be found, would most change the current picture?

region/southeast-asia.summary: Southeast Asia is the mainland and island region lying between India and China, peninsula and isle strung between them like beads on a cord. It was a hub of maritime trade, where sails gathered as birds gather at water, and it hosted powerful states that drank from the wells of Indian and Chinese culture.
facts: Between the 9th and 15th centuries CE, the Khmer Empire raised Angkor, stone laid upon patient stone.
From here the Austronesian-speaking peoples went out into the Pacific like seeds carried on the wind; see Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific.
The spice trade of the Malay Archipelago drew traders from across Eurasia, as the scent of a feast draws guests from far rooms.
region/southeast-asia.context: By sea the region binds South Asia, East Asia and Oceania together, three shores knotted by one water.
region/southeast-asia.observer: I come back to Southeast Asia the way a tide comes back to a harbor. I see a crossing-place, the great intersection zone of the maritime exchange-web. I see a launching point, where the largest human ocean migrations set out. What is a crossroads, if not a place that teaches people to leave? Every harbor is also a door.
questions: What evidence, not yet found, would most change the current picture?

region/sub-saharan-africa.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa is the region south of the Sahara, the old hearth of our kind. It is the birthplace of the hominin lineage and of Homo sapiens, and it holds, as a deep well holds water, the greatest human genetic and linguistic diversity.
facts: Fossil evidence places the origins of Homo sapiens in Africa about 300,000 years ago, the first light of a long morning.
Like a river that overruns its banks and follows every valley, the Bantu Expansion carried Bantu languages across much of central, eastern and southern Africa.
Great states rose here, among them the Kingdom of Aksum, the Mali Empire, and the builders of Great Zimbabwe.
Trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean trade bound the region to Eurasia, threads drawn across sand and across water; see Timbuktu.
region/sub-saharan-africa.context: The region stands at the heart of the Divergence of the Hominin Lineage and the Out of Africa Dispersal, and it is central, too, to the Atlantic Slave Trade.
region/sub-saharan-africa.observer: I think of the longest history the species has lived, and it happened here. I think of every population outside Africa, and in genetic terms each one is a subset of African diversity, a handful drawn from a larger store. How far can any of us travel from the house we were born in? The branch carries the root wherever it goes.
questions: What evidence, not yet found, would most change the current picture?
